The history of the Roman Empire is a vast narrative spanning over a millennium, evolving from a small city-state on the Italian Peninsula into the dominant superpower of the ancient world. Its story begins not with an empire, but with a kingdom. According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE by the twins Romulus and Remus, descendants of the Trojan hero Aeneas. Romulus, after killing his brother in a dispute over leadership, became the first king of Rome. Under the rule of seven successive kings, Rome grew from a collection of Latin villages into a formidable city, developing early institutions such as the Senate and establishing a distinct social hierarchy divided between patricians (aristocrats) and plebeians (commoners).

However, the monarchy ended in 509 BCE when the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled due to his tyrannical rule. This event marked the birth of the Roman Republic (*Res Publica*), a system designed to prevent the concentration of power in a single individual. The Republic was governed by two consuls elected annually, who shared executive authority and were checked by the Senate and various assemblies. During the next two centuries, Rome engaged in a series of grueling conflicts to secure its dominance over the Italian peninsula, including the wars against the Samnites and the Greek colonies in the south. By the third century BCE, Rome turned its gaze outward, clashing with Carthage, the great maritime power of the western Mediterranean, in the Punic Wars. The victory in these wars, particularly through the leadership of Scipio Africanus, catapulted Rome into a hegemonic power, granting it control over Spain, North Africa, and the islands of the western Mediterranean.

As Rome's territory expanded, so did its internal tensions. The influx of wealth and slaves disrupted the traditional agrarian economy, leading to widespread social unrest
